interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 description BR12-AP01
 switchport access vlan 50
 switchport mode access
 spanning-tree portfast
end
choices: Make Gi1/0/10 a trunk with native VLAN 50 and allow VLANs 12 and 50.
Change the port to access VLAN 12 so STAFF traffic lands in the right VLAN.
Change the AP to local mode so STAFF traffic is switched at the branch.
Create VLAN 12 as a dynamic interface on the WLC, because locally switched WLANs use the controller's VLANs.
explanation: A FlexConnect AP that locally switches a WLAN puts that traffic on the wired port tagged with the WLAN's VLAN, so the switch port must be a trunk that allows VLAN 12; the AP's own management traffic stays untagged, so the native VLAN should be the AP management VLAN 50. GUEST works because it is tunneled in CAPWAP over the management VLAN. Moving the port to VLAN 12 would cut the AP off from its management subnet, local mode tunnels everything to the WLC, and locally switched traffic never touches the WLC's interfaces.

stem: Which two statements describe TACACS+ when compared with RADIUS? (Choose two.)
choices: It uses TCP port 49.
It uses UDP ports 1812 and 1813.
It encrypts the entire body of each packet.
It combines authentication and authorization in one exchange.
It encrypts only the password in the access request.
explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, encrypts the whole packet body, and keeps authentication, authorization and accounting separate, which suits per-command authorization for device administration. RADIUS uses UDP 1812 and 1813 (1645 and 1646 on older systems), encrypts only the password, and combines authentication and authorization.

stem: Laptops that use DHCP connect to the LAB-IOT WLAN and work normally. Several sensors with static IP addresses in the correct VLAN 330 subnet complete the PSK handshake but cannot pass any traffic. Based on the AireOS WLAN settings in the exhibit, which change lets the sensors work?
exhibit:
WLANs > Edit 'LAB-IOT'  (AireOS WLC)

General   Status: [x] Enabled   SSID: LAB-IOT   Broadcast SSID: [x] Enabled
          Interface/Interface Group(G): iot-vlan330
Security  Layer 2 Security: WPA2   Encryption: AES   Auth Key Mgmt: PSK
QoS       Quality of Service (QoS): Silver (best effort)
Advanced  Allow AAA Override: [ ] Enabled
          Enable Session Timeout: [x] 1800 sec
          DHCP Server: [ ] Override
          DHCP Addr. Assignment: [x] Required
          Client Exclusion: [x] Enabled  Timeout Value: 60 sec
choices: Enable Allow AAA Override.
Clear the DHCP Addr. Assignment Required check box.
Change the QoS profile to Platinum.
Disable Client Exclusion.
explanation: With DHCP Addr. Assignment Required checked, the WLC lets a client pass traffic only after it obtains an address through DHCP, so clients with static addresses stay stuck even though they authenticated. Clearing that option fixes the sensors. AAA override only applies attributes from a RADIUS server, QoS does not block traffic, and client exclusion is triggered by repeated authentication failures, which is not what is happening here.

stem: A packet destined for 10.20.5.77 arrives on R1's GigabitEthernet0/0. Based on the exhibit, to which next-hop address does R1 forward it?
exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 5 masks
C        10.0.12.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
C        10.0.14.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.14.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
D        10.20.4.0/22 [90/30720] via 10.0.13.3, 01:02:44, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.20.5.0/25 [1/0] via 10.0.14.4
O        10.20.5.64/26 [110/4] via 10.0.12.2, 00:18:09, GigabitEthernet0/1
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
explanation: 10.20.5.77 is covered by three routes: 10.20.4.0/22 (10.20.4.0 to 10.20.7.255), 10.20.5.0/25 (.0 to .127) and 10.20.5.64/26 (.64 to .127). The router always picks the longest matching prefix first, so the OSPF /26 via 10.0.12.2 wins. The static route's AD of 1 is irrelevant here, because administrative distance only breaks ties between routes for the exact same prefix and length. The EIGRP /22 and the default route are less specific, so they are used only for addresses that the longer routes do not cover.

stem: Refer to the exhibit. Every interface runs at the speed shown, and no interface has a manual ip ospf cost or bandwidth command. What metric does R1 list in its routing table for 192.168.30.0/24?
exhibit:
All routers:
 router ospf 1
  auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
 (all other OSPF settings are default; all links in area 0)

R1 Te0/0/0 (10 Gbps)   ----  Te0/0/0 R4
R4 Gi0/0/1 (1 Gbps)    ----  Gi0/0/1 R3
R1 Gi0/0/1 (1 Gbps)    ----  Gi0/0/1 R2
R2 Fa0/1/0 (100 Mbps)  ----  Fa0/1/0 R3
R3 Gi0/0/0 (1 Gbps)    ----  LAN 192.168.30.0/24
explanation: With a reference bandwidth of 10000 Mbps, interface cost is 10000 divided by the interface bandwidth in Mbps: 10 Gbps = 1, 1 Gbps = 10, 100 Mbps = 100. OSPF adds the cost of each outgoing interface along the path, including R3's interface onto the destination LAN. Through R4 the cost is 1 + 10 + 10 = 21; through R2 it is 10 + 100 + 10 = 120. OSPF installs the lowest-cost path, so R1 shows [110/21]. With the default 100 Mbps reference, every one of these links would cost 1 and the two paths would tie.

stem: Match each route source to its default administrative distance on a Cisco IOS router.
pairs: Static route that uses a next-hop address
explanation: Cisco default ADs: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP internal 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, EIGRP external 170, iBGP 200, and 255 for a source that is not trusted at all. 100 is not the default for any of these sources, and 200 belongs to internal BGP, which is not listed. Lower AD is more trusted when two sources offer the same prefix.

stem: Refer to the exhibit from R1. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
192.0.2.4         1   FULL/DR         00:00:36    10.5.0.4        GigabitEthernet0/0
192.0.2.3         1   FULL/BDR        00:00:31    10.5.0.3        GigabitEthernet0/0
192.0.2.2         0   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:39    10.5.0.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
172.31.0.9        0   FULL/  -        00:00:34    10.9.0.2        GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: R1 is neither the DR nor the BDR on the GigabitEthernet0/0 segment.
The neighbor 192.0.2.2 cannot become DR or BDR on this segment with its current configuration.
The 2WAY state with 192.0.2.2 points to a hello or dead timer mismatch that must be fixed.
GigabitEthernet0/1 is a broadcast network on which R1 was elected DR.
R1 is missing the routes behind 192.0.2.2, because the two routers never exchange LSAs directly.
explanation: The DR (192.0.2.4) and BDR (192.0.2.3) are other routers, so R1 is a DROTHER. 192.0.2.2 has priority 0, which makes it ineligible for DR or BDR. Two DROTHERs normally stop at 2-WAY with each other and become FULL only with the DR and BDR, so 2WAY is not a fault, and R1 still learns 192.0.2.2's LSAs through the DR. The FULL/- state on Gi0/1 means no DR/BDR exists there, which is the point-to-point network type, not broadcast.

stem: R1 and R2 connect through their GigabitEthernet0/0 interfaces on the same switch VLAN. They can ping each other, but show ip ospf neighbor is empty on both routers. Which change fixes the problem?
exhibit:
R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.12.1 255.255.255.0
!
router ospf 10
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0

R2
interface Loopback0
 ip address 10.20.20.2 255.255.255.255
 ip ospf 20 area 0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.12.2 255.255.255.128
 ip ospf 20 area 0
!
router ospf 20
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 passive-interface Loopback0
choices: On R2, change the GigabitEthernet0/0 address to 10.1.12.2 255.255.255.0.
On R2, replace router ospf 20 with router ospf 10 so the process IDs match.
On R2, remove ip ospf 20 area 0 from GigabitEthernet0/0 and add network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 under the OSPF process.
On R2, remove passive-interface Loopback0.
explanation: On a broadcast network, OSPF hellos carry the interface subnet mask and both sides must agree. R1 uses /24 and R2 uses /25, so each router ignores the other's hellos. Ping still works because 10.1.12.1 falls inside R2's 10.1.12.0/25 and 10.1.12.2 falls inside R1's /24. Process IDs are locally significant, enabling OSPF with the interface command works the same as a network statement, and making the loopback passive has no effect on GigabitEthernet0/0.

stem: Refer to the exhibit from branch router R2. Which statement describes R2's default route?
exhibit:
R2# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.9 to network 0.0.0.0

O*E2  0.0.0.0/0 [110/1] via 10.0.0.9, 02:14:51, GigabitEthernet0/0
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 5 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.0.0.8/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.0.10/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.30.0.0/24 [110/2] via 10.0.0.9, 02:14:51, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.31.0.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.31.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: It was learned through OSPF as an external route, injected by a router that advertises a default route into OSPF (for example with default-information originate).
It is a static default route configured on R2 with an administrative distance of 110.
Its metric of 1 means the Internet edge router is one hop away from R2.
R2 drops packets for unknown destinations, because an external OSPF route cannot serve as the gateway of last resort.
explanation: O means OSPF, the asterisk marks a candidate default, and E2 means an external type 2 route, which an ASBR injects, typically with default-information originate. A static route would show the code S. E2 routes keep the seed metric set by the ASBR (1 by default for a default route) no matter how far away it is, so the metric is not a hop count. The Gateway of last resort line shows that R2 does use this route for unknown destinations.

stem: Branch router R1 receives its default route from OSPF. A backup Internet circuit connects R1's GigabitEthernet0/2 to the ISP router at 198.51.100.1. Enter the global configuration command that adds a backup IPv4 default route through that ISP. It must use the lowest administrative distance that still keeps it out of the routing table while the OSPF default route exists.
exhibit:
R1# show ip route | include 0.0.0.0/0
O*E2  0.0.0.0/0 [110/1] via 10.0.0.1, 00:45:10, GigabitEthernet0/0

R1# show ip interface brief | include GigabitEthernet0/2
GigabitEthernet0/2     198.51.100.2    YES manual up                    up
explanation: A floating static route needs an administrative distance higher than the route it backs up. OSPF routes have AD 110, so 111 is the lowest value that keeps the static route out of the table until the OSPF default disappears. Without a distance the static route would get AD 1 and replace the OSPF default immediately, and a distance of exactly 110 would tie with OSPF instead of floating behind it.

stem: R2 was given HSRP priority 120 so that it would become the active gateway for VLAN 20, but R1 is still active. Which change makes R2 the active router without reloading either router?
exhibit:
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/1       20   100   Active  local           10.20.0.3       10.20.0.1

R2# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/1       20   120   Standby 10.20.0.2       local           10.20.0.1
choices: Configure standby 20 preempt on R2's GigabitEthernet0/1.
Configure standby 20 preempt on R1's GigabitEthernet0/1.
Raise R2's priority further with standby 20 priority 255.
Configure standby version 2 on R2 so that it can claim the active role.
explanation: HSRP preemption is disabled by default, so a router with a higher priority does not take over from an active router that is already working. The empty P column shows that neither router preempts. Preempt must be on the router that should take over, R2; preempt on R1 does nothing because R1 has the lower priority. Raising the priority to 255 still needs preempt, and changing only R2 to version 2 would stop the routers from hearing each other's hellos.

stem: R3 receives a packet for 2001:DB8:ACAD:4F::10. Which next hop and outgoing interface does R3 use?
exhibit:
R3# show ipv6 route
IPv6 Routing Table - default - 8 entries
Codes: C - Connected, L - Local, S - Static, U - Per-user Static route
       B - BGP, R - RIP, O - OSPF Intra, OI - OSPF Inter
       OE1 - OSPF ext 1, OE2 - OSPF ext 2 (remaining codes omitted)
S   ::/0 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FFFF::1
S   2001:DB8:ACAD::/48 [1/0]
     via FE80::5, GigabitEthernet0/0/1
O   2001:DB8:ACAD:40::/58 [110/3]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0/2
S   2001:DB8:ACAD:48::/61 [1/0]
     via FE80::4, GigabitEthernet0/0/3
O   2001:DB8:ACAD:4E::/64 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0/2
C   2001:DB8:FFFF::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/0, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:FFFF::2/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/0, receive
L   FF00::/8 [0/0]
     via Null0, receive
choices: FE80::4 out GigabitEthernet0/0/3
FE80::2 out GigabitEthernet0/0/2
FE80::5 out GigabitEthernet0/0/1
2001:DB8:FFFF::1 out GigabitEthernet0/0/0
explanation: The fourth hextet of the destination is 004F. The /64 for 4E does not match, because a /64 needs the whole fourth hextet to be 004E. The /61 fixes the top 13 bits of that hextet and covers 0048 to 004F, so it matches; the /58 covers 0040 to 007F and the /48 and ::/0 also match. Longest prefix match selects the /61 static route via FE80::4 on GigabitEthernet0/0/3.

stem: R5 and R6 are joined by a new point-to-point link with OSPF enabled on both ends. Put the OSPF neighbor states that R5 moves through for R6 in order, from first to last, until the adjacency is complete.
items: Down
Init
2-Way
ExStart
Exchange
Loading
Full
explanation: Init means R5 has received a hello from R6 that does not yet list R5's router ID; 2-Way means each router sees its own ID in the other's hello. In ExStart the routers pick master and slave for the database exchange, in Exchange they swap DBD summaries, in Loading they request and receive the LSAs they lack, and Full means the databases are synchronized. On a point-to-point link there is no DR election, so the routers continue straight past 2-Way.

stem: A site is replacing one of its two Cisco gateway routers with a router from another vendor, so the team will move the gateway pair from HSRP to VRRP. Which two statements about VRRP are true? (Choose two.)
choices: VRRP is an IETF standard, so routers from both vendors can join the same group.
Preemption is on by default, so a backup with a higher priority than the current master takes over without extra configuration.
The router that forwards traffic is called the active router, and the waiting router is the standby router.
A single VRRP group spreads hosts across both routers by answering ARP requests with different virtual MAC addresses.
VRRP routers send their advertisements to 224.0.0.2.
explanation: VRRP is an open standard (RFC 5798), so it works between vendors, and unlike HSRP it preempts by default. VRRP calls its roles master and backup; active and standby are HSRP terms. Handing out different virtual MACs from one group to share load is how GLBP works. VRRP advertisements go to 224.0.0.18, while 224.0.0.2 is used by HSRP version 1.

stem: R1 (router ID 10.255.0.1) and R2 (router ID 10.255.0.2) share a link. Several minutes after the link came up, R2 still shows the output in the exhibit. Which change on R2's GigabitEthernet0/0 lets the adjacency reach FULL?
exhibit:
R2# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
10.255.0.1        1   EXSTART/BDR     00:00:36    10.12.0.1       GigabitEthernet0/0

R2# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU is 1400 bytes

R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU is 1500 bytes
choices: ip mtu 1500
ip ospf network point-to-point
ip ospf priority 0
ip ospf dead-interval 40
explanation: A neighbor stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE is the classic sign of an IP MTU mismatch. DBD packets carry the interface MTU, and a router rejects DBDs that advertise an MTU larger than its own, so the database exchange never finishes. Matching the MTU at 1500 fixes it (ip ospf mtu-ignore on both sides is a workaround). A timer mismatch would stop the routers before 2-Way, so they would not appear at all; the network type and priority do not affect the MTU check.

stem: R5 has just booted with the configuration shown. Which OSPF router ID does R5 use?
exhibit:
R5# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     172.31.200.1    YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.0.56.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Loopback0              10.0.0.5        YES manual up                    up
Loopback1              192.168.255.5   YES manual administratively down down

R5# show running-config | section router ospf
router ospf 1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0
explanation: With no router-id command, IOS uses the highest IPv4 address on a loopback interface that is up, and only falls back to physical interfaces when no loopback is up. Loopback1 has the highest loopback address but is administratively down, so it is skipped, leaving Loopback0, 10.0.0.5. GigabitEthernet0/0's 172.31.200.1 is higher, but a loopback that is up always takes precedence over a physical interface. The loopback does not need to be advertised in OSPF to supply the router ID.

stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two statements about how R1 forwards traffic are true? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.0.12.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.13.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
O        10.50.0.0/16 [110/21] via 10.0.12.2, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/1
                      [110/21] via 10.0.13.3, 00:03:11, GigabitEthernet0/2
S        10.50.8.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.13.3
choices: R1 can forward traffic for 10.50.0.0/16 out both GigabitEthernet0/1 and GigabitEthernet0/2, because both paths have the same OSPF cost.
A packet for 10.50.8.20 is forwarded only to 10.0.13.3.
Traffic for 10.50.0.0/16 uses only 10.0.12.2, because that path is listed first.
The value 21 is the number of router hops to 10.50.0.0/16.
A packet for 10.50.9.1 uses the static route, because its administrative distance of 1 is lower than OSPF's 110.
explanation: Two next hops with the same [110/21] are equal-cost paths, and OSPF installs up to four by default, so R1 shares the load across both. 10.50.8.20 matches the /24 static route, which is longer than the /16, so it goes only to 10.0.13.3. The order of the lines does not make one path primary, and 21 is the cumulative OSPF cost, not a hop count. 10.50.9.1 is outside 10.50.8.0/24, so the static route never matches it and AD is never compared.

stem: R1, R2, R3 and R4 connect to the same VLAN through GigabitEthernet0/0 and run OSPF area 0 on it. All other settings are default, and all four routers start at the same moment. Which routers become the DR and the BDR?
exhibit:
R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf priority 0
router ospf 1
 router-id 172.16.0.1

R2
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.0.0.2

R3
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf priority 50
router ospf 1
 router-id 3.3.3.3

R4
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.4.4.4
choices: DR: R3, BDR: R4
DR: R1, BDR: R4
DR: R4, BDR: R2
DR: R3, BDR: R1
explanation: The highest interface priority wins first, so R3 (priority 50) becomes DR even though its router ID is the lowest. R1 has the highest router ID, but priority 0 makes it ineligible for DR or BDR. R2 and R4 tie at the default priority of 1, so the higher router ID, R4's 10.4.4.4, becomes BDR. Router ID is only a tie-breaker after priority.

stem: R1 must reach 2001:DB8:20::/64 through R2. On the shared Ethernet link, R2's interface has only a link-local address, FE80::2, and R1 connects to that link on GigabitEthernet0/1. IPv6 unicast routing is enabled. Which command creates a working static route on R1?
choices: ipv6 route 2001:DB8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:20::/64 FE80::2 GigabitEthernet0/1
ip route 2001:DB8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::2
explanation: A link-local address is only unique on one link, so an IPv6 static route that uses a link-local next hop must also name the exit interface, and IOS expects the interface before the address. Without the interface, IOS rejects the command; with the interface after the address, the syntax is wrong. The ip route command configures IPv4 routes only.

stem: The primary ISP's router has failed, but R1's GigabitEthernet0/0 connects to it through a provider switch and stays up. Internet traffic is now dropped instead of using the backup ISP. What explains this behavior?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ip route
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 5

R1# show ip interface brief | include GigabitEthernet0/[01]
GigabitEthernet0/0     203.0.113.2     YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     198.51.100.2    YES manual up                    up

R1# show ip route static | begin Gateway
Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1

R1# ping 203.0.113.1
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 203.0.113.1, timeout is 2 seconds:
.....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
choices: The primary static route stays installed because its next hop is still inside a connected subnet on an up/up interface; IOS does not remove a static route just because the next hop stops responding.
The backup route can never be installed, because an administrative distance of 5 is too low for a floating static route.
The backup route needs the permanent keyword before it can be installed when the primary route fails.
The two static default routes are load-balanced, so half of the traffic is still sent to the failed ISP router.
explanation: A static route stays in the table as long as its next hop resolves, here through the connected 203.0.113.0 subnet on an up/up interface. The floating route (AD 5, higher than 1, so it floats correctly) is installed only after the primary route is removed, for example when Gi0/0 goes down. The permanent keyword does the opposite: it keeps a route even when its interface fails. The routes are not equal-cost, because their ADs differ and only one S* line is installed. Detecting a dead next hop on a link that stays up needs object tracking such as IP SLA.

stem: Refer to the exhibit from the active router. Hosts in VLAN 45 send ARP requests for their default gateway, 10.45.0.1. Which MAC address appears in the ARP reply? Use the format xxxx.xxxx.xxxx.
exhibit:
interface Vlan45
 ip address 10.45.0.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 45 ip 10.45.0.1
 standby 45 priority 110
 standby 45 preempt
explanation: The active HSRP router answers ARP for the virtual IP with the virtual MAC. HSRP version 2 builds it as 0000.0C9F.F000 plus the group number in hex (groups 0 to 4095), and 45 decimal is 2D hex, giving 0000.0C9F.F02D. HSRP version 1 would use 0000.0C07.AC2D, and VRRP group 45 would use 0000.5E00.012D.

stem: R1 learns, or is configured with, the routes in the exhibit. Which next hop does R1 use for a packet to 192.168.80.200?
explanation: 192.168.80.0/25 covers only .0 to .127, so it does not match .200, and the remaining candidates are all /24s. For the same prefix, the router installs the source with the lowest administrative distance: EIGRP 90 beats the static route at 95 and OSPF at 110. Metrics from different protocols (2816 versus cost 2) are never compared with each other.

stem: R7 and R8 connect through a switch on VLAN 78, and both have OSPF enabled on their VLAN 78 interfaces. Which two configuration differences would stop them from becoming OSPF neighbors? (Choose two.)
choices: R7 uses OSPF process ID 1 and R8 uses process ID 100.
R7 has ip ospf hello-interval 5 on the interface and R8 uses the default hello interval.
R7 places the interface in area 0 and R8 places it in area 78.
R7 has interface priority 0 and R8 has priority 1.
R7 uses auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 and R8 uses the default.
R7's router ID is 7.7.7.7 and R8's router ID is 8.8.8.8.
explanation: Neighbors must agree on the hello and dead intervals, the area ID, the subnet and mask, authentication and stub flags, so a hello interval of 5 versus 10 and area 0 versus area 78 both block the adjacency. Process IDs are local to each router. Priority 0 only removes R7 from the DR/BDR election. A different reference bandwidth changes costs but not adjacency, and router IDs must be different, not equal.

stem: Users on 10.1.1.0/24 behind R1 cannot reach server 10.3.3.10 behind R3, even though R1 has an OSPF route to 10.3.3.0/24 through R2. R2 is configured correctly. Which command, added under router ospf 1 on R1, fixes the problem?

R1# show running-config | section interface|router ospf
interface GigabitEthernet0/0

interface GigabitEthernet0/1

router ospf 1

R3# show ip route

       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 3 masks

choices: default-information originate
passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
explanation: R1's statement network 10.1.0.0 0.0.0.255 matches only 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.0.255, so Gi0/0 (10.1.1.1) is not in OSPF and 10.1.1.0/24 is never advertised. R3's table has no route back to 10.1.1.0/24 and no default, so replies from the server are dropped. The wildcard 0.0.255.0 matches only addresses whose last octet is 0, so it still misses 10.1.1.1. default-information originate does nothing because R1 has no default route of its own, and passive-interface affects only interfaces that are already in OSPF.

stem: Match each IPv4 routing table code to what it identifies.
pairs: An address configured on one of this router's own interfaces, shown as a /32
A subnet attached to one of this router's up/up interfaces
A static route that is a candidate default route
An OSPF route to a prefix in a different area
An OSPF external route whose metric does not grow inside the OSPF domain
explanation: L (local) entries are the router's own interface addresses as /32 host routes, and C entries are the connected subnets. S is static and the asterisk marks a candidate default. O is OSPF intra-area, O IA is inter-area, and O E2 is an external type 2 route whose metric stays at the seed value. D is EIGRP; RIP uses the code R, which is not listed.

stem: The primary circuit on GigabitEthernet0/0/0 is down. GigabitEthernet0/0/1 is up/up, and the backup ISP's router answers pings on that link. R1 has no other routing source, and the exhibit shows that R1 has no IPv6 default route. Why?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config
(output omitted)
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description Primary ISP
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:A::2/64
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description Backup ISP
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:B:1::2/64
!
(output omitted)
ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/0/0 FE80::1
ipv6 route ::/0 2001:DB8:B::1 210
(output omitted)

R1# show ipv6 route static
IPv6 Routing Table - default - 3 entries
Codes: C - Connected, L - Local, S - Static, U - Per-user Static route
       (remaining codes omitted)

R1#
choices: The backup route's next hop, 2001:DB8:B::1, is not inside any connected prefix (Gi0/0/1 is on 2001:DB8:B:1::/64), so IOS cannot resolve it and does not install the route.
An IPv6 static route cannot use an administrative distance higher than 200.
An IPv6 default static route must always include an exit interface.
A floating static route is installed only after the router is reloaded.
explanation: 2001:DB8:B::1 expands to 2001:DB8:B:0::1, which is in 2001:DB8:B::/64, not in the connected 2001:DB8:B:1::/64. With the primary interface down, R1 has no route that covers that next hop, so the backup route stays unresolved and out of the table. Correcting the next hop to the backup router's real address on 2001:DB8:B:1::/64 fixes it. IPv6 static routes accept distances from 1 to 254, an exit interface is needed only for a link-local next hop, and floating routes are installed as soon as they win, with no reload.

stem: R1 reaches 172.20.8.0/24 through OSPF, as shown. For a test, only traffic to the server 172.20.8.25 must go to the firewall at 10.9.9.6, while the rest of 172.20.8.0/24 keeps following OSPF. Enter the static route command that does this.
exhibit:
R1# show ip route 172.20.8.0
Routing entry for 172.20.8.0/24
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 3, type intra area
  Last update from 10.9.9.2 on GigabitEthernet0/1, 00:22:10 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.9.9.2, from 172.20.255.1, 00:22:10 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/1
      Route metric is 3, traffic share count is 1
explanation: A host route uses the mask 255.255.255.255 (/32), which is longer than the OSPF /24, so longest prefix match sends only 172.20.8.25 to 10.9.9.6. Both routes stay in the table because they are different prefixes, so their administrative distances are never compared. A /24 static route would instead replace the OSPF route for the whole subnet, because static AD 1 beats OSPF's 110.

stem: Refer to the exhibit from R2 in a single-area OSPF network. Which statement is correct?
exhibit:
R2# show ip ospf database

            OSPF Router with ID (2.2.2.2) (Process ID 1)

                Router Link States (Area 0)

Link ID         ADV Router      Age         Seq#       Checksum Link count
1.1.1.1         1.1.1.1         1208        0x80000007 0x00B2C1 2
2.2.2.2         2.2.2.2         1190        0x80000009 0x00D4E3 3
3.3.3.3         3.3.3.3         1185        0x80000006 0x0091A7 2
4.4.4.4         4.4.4.4         1179        0x80000005 0x004E2F 1

                Net Link States (Area 0)

Link ID         ADV Router      Age         Seq#       Checksum
10.1.123.3      3.3.3.3         1185        0x80000003 0x00C8D0
choices: The router with ID 3.3.3.3 is the DR for a multiaccess segment, and 10.1.123.3 is its interface address on that segment.
The router with ID 2.2.2.2 is the DR, because it reports the highest link count.
Area 0 contains five routers: four router LSAs plus one network LSA.
10.1.123.3 is the router ID of R3, taken from its highest interface address.
explanation: Only the DR originates a network (type 2) LSA for a multiaccess segment. Its Link ID is the DR's interface IP on that segment and its ADV Router is the DR's router ID, so 3.3.3.3 is the DR, using 10.1.123.3. Each router originates exactly one router (type 1) LSA, so there are four routers; the network LSA describes a segment, not a router. Link count reflects how many links a router describes, not its DR role, and the router IDs are the Link IDs of the router LSAs.

The default route is used only when nothing more specific matches.

stem: R1 and R2 run OSPF with all default settings, and the serial link is R1's only path to R2. What metric does R1 show in its routing table for 10.22.0.0/24?
exhibit:
R1 S0/0/0 -------- S0/0/0 R2 Gi0/0 -------- LAN 10.22.0.0/24

R1# show interfaces Serial0/0/0 | include BW
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1544 Kbit/sec, DLY 20000 usec,

R2# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include BW
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
explanation: The default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps (100000 kbps). The serial interface costs 100000 / 1544 = 64.77, which IOS truncates to 64, and the Gigabit LAN interface costs 1 because the cost can never be lower than 1. OSPF adds the outgoing interface costs along the path, including R2's interface onto the LAN, so R1 shows [110/65].

stem: R1 and R2 are directly connected on GigabitEthernet0/0, and OSPF has not formed an adjacency on that link. Which two changes are both needed so the routers become fully adjacent? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 172.16.12.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 ip ospf 1 area 0
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1

R2
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 172.16.12.2 255.255.255.252
!
router ospf 7
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 passive-interface default
 no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 network 172.16.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
choices: On R2, under router ospf 7, add no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0.
On R1, under GigabitEthernet0/0, add no ip ospf hello-interval 5.
On R2, change the process to router ospf 1 to match R1.
On R1, add network 172.16.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 under router ospf 1.
On R2, add ip ospf dead-interval 20 under GigabitEthernet0/0.
explanation: passive-interface default makes every R2 interface passive except Gi0/1, so R2 sends no hellos on Gi0/0. R1 also uses a 5-second hello, which makes its dead interval 20 automatically, while R2 uses 10 and 40, and both values must match. Setting only the dead interval on R2 still leaves the hello intervals different. Process IDs are locally significant, and R1's interface is already enabled with ip ospf 1 area 0, so a network statement adds nothing.

stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which statement about R4 is correct?
exhibit:
R4# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Lo0          1     0               10.255.255.4/32    1     LOOP  0/0
Gi0/2        1     0               10.0.24.4/24       1     BDR   2/2
Gi0/1        1     0               10.0.34.2/30       1     P2P   1/1
Gi0/0        1     0               10.40.0.1/24       1     DR    0/0
choices: Gi0/1 uses the OSPF point-to-point network type, so no DR or BDR is elected on that link.
R4 is the DR on Gi0/0 because it is fully adjacent with every router on that segment.
On Gi0/2, R4 has two neighbors but is fully adjacent with only one of them.
Lo0 is in the LOOP state, so its address is not advertised into OSPF.
explanation: P2P in the State column is the point-to-point network type, which has no DR/BDR election. Gi0/0 shows 0/0, meaning no OSPF neighbors at all; R4 is DR there only because it is alone on the segment (a good candidate for passive-interface). F/C means fully adjacent over total neighbors, so 2/2 on Gi0/2 means the BDR is FULL with both neighbors, as a BDR should be. A loopback in the LOOP state is still advertised, as a /32 host route by default.

stem: R1 and R2 booted together and R1 became the active router. Later, R1's GigabitEthernet0/1 went down for ten minutes and then came back up. Which router is active for group 30 after R1's interface recovers, and why?
exhibit:
R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.30.0.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 30 ip 10.30.0.1
 standby 30 priority 110

R2
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.30.0.3 255.255.255.0
 standby 30 ip 10.30.0.1
 standby 30 preempt
choices: R2, because R1 is not configured to preempt and so cannot take the active role back.
R1, because its priority of 110 is higher than R2's default priority of 100.
R1, because R2's preempt setting makes R2 hand the active role to any router with a higher priority.
R2, because the router with the higher interface IP address always becomes active.
explanation: While R1 was down, R2 became active. A recovering router takes the active role back only if it has preempt configured, and R1 does not, so R1 settles as standby despite its higher priority. Preempt on R2 lets R2 take over from a lower-priority active router; it does not make R2 give the role away. The higher IP address is only a tie-breaker when priorities are equal.

stem: Put the sources that an IOS router uses to choose its OSPF router ID in order of precedence, from highest to lowest.
items: The router-id command under the OSPF process
The highest IPv4 address on a loopback interface that is up
The highest IPv4 address on a non-loopback interface that is up
explanation: A manually configured router-id always wins. Without it, IOS takes the highest IPv4 address on an up loopback, and only when no loopback is up does it use the highest IPv4 address on an up physical interface. The choice is made when the process starts, so a later change needs clear ip ospf process or a reload.

stem: Each virtual MAC address below belongs to group 10 of a first hop redundancy protocol. Match each address to the protocol that uses it.
explanation: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0C07.ACxx and HSRPv2 uses 0000.0C9F.Fxxx, with the group number in hex (10 = 0A). VRRP uses 0000.5E00.01xx. GLBP uses 0007.B400.XXYY, where XX is the group and YY is the forwarder (AVF) number, so 0007.B400.0A01 is group 10, forwarder 1.

exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ip route
ip route 10.60.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.2 120

R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 7 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
C        10.0.99.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.0.99.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
S        10.60.0.0/16 [120/0] via 10.0.99.2
O        10.60.0.0/17 [110/3] via 10.0.12.2, 00:52:30, GigabitEthernet0/1
O        10.60.128.0/17 [110/3] via 10.0.12.2, 00:52:30, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: The static route is installed because no other source offers exactly 10.60.0.0/16, but traffic to 10.60.200.5 still follows OSPF to 10.0.12.2 because the /17 is a longer match.
All traffic to 10.60.0.0/16 now uses 10.0.99.2, because the static route covers the whole range.
The table is in an error state, because a floating static route can appear only after the OSPF routes are removed.
Traffic to 10.60.200.5 is load-balanced between 10.0.12.2 and 10.0.99.2.
explanation: Administrative distance is compared only between routes for the identical prefix and length. OSPF advertises two /17s, not the /16, so the static /16 has no competitor and is installed despite its AD of 120. Longest prefix match still sends 10.60.200.5 through the OSPF 10.60.128.0/17. The static route still acts as a backup in practice: if a /17 disappears, traffic for that half falls through to the /16. There is no load balancing between routes of different lengths.

stem: On a VLAN that already has an elected DR and BDR, an engineer adds a new OSPF router, R9, with ip ospf priority 255 on its interface. Every other router on the VLAN uses the default priority. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
choices: R9 does not become DR when it joins; the existing DR keeps its role.
If the current DR later fails, the current BDR becomes DR and R9 is elected BDR.
R9 becomes DR as soon as it joins, because 255 is the highest possible priority.
If the current DR later fails, R9 becomes DR directly because it has the highest priority on the segment.
R9 forms a FULL adjacency only with the DR and stays in 2-WAY with the BDR.
explanation: OSPF DR/BDR election is not preemptive, so a new router with a higher priority does not displace a working DR or BDR. When the DR fails, the BDR is promoted to DR and a new BDR election is held among the eligible routers, which R9 wins with priority 255. Every DROTHER, including R9, becomes FULL with both the DR and the BDR.

stem: Which statement describes how R2 forwards packets to 2001:DB8:CAFE:10::25 and to 2001:DB8:CAFE:10::26?
exhibit:
R2# show ipv6 route
IPv6 Routing Table - default - 7 entries
Codes: C - Connected, L - Local, S - Static, U - Per-user Static route
       (remaining codes omitted)
S   ::/0 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:0:F::1
C   2001:DB8:0:F::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/0, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:0:F::2/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/0, receive
C   2001:DB8:CAFE:10::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/1, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:CAFE:10::1/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0/1, receive
S   2001:DB8:CAFE:10::25/128 [1/0]
     via FE80::9, GigabitEthernet0/0/2
L   FF00::/8 [0/0]
     via Null0, receive
choices: The ::25 packet goes to FE80::9 out Gi0/0/2, and the ::26 packet is delivered directly out Gi0/0/1.
Both are delivered directly out Gi0/0/1, because a connected route (AD 0) is always preferred over a static route.
Both go to FE80::9 out Gi0/0/2, because the static route takes over the whole subnet.
The ::25 packet is sent out both Gi0/0/1 and Gi0/0/2, because two routes match it.
explanation: The /128 static host route is a longer match than the connected /64, so ::25 follows the host route to FE80::9. ::26 matches only the connected /64 (and the default), so it is delivered on Gi0/0/1. Administrative distance would matter only if both routes had the same prefix length, and a router forwards each packet out a single best path, not every matching route.

stem: R2 was built from a copy of R1's configuration, and the two routers will not form an OSPF adjacency. Which action on R2 fixes the problem?
exhibit:
R2# show running-config | section router ospf
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.0.0.1
 network 10.12.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 10.2.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0

R1# show ip ospf | include ID
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.0.0.1

R1# show logging | include OSPF
*Oct 21 14:02:11.517: %OSPF-4-DUP_RTRID_NBR: OSPF detected duplicate router-id 10.0.0.1 from 10.12.0.2 on interface GigabitEthernet0/0
choices: Enter router-id 10.0.0.2 under router ospf 1, and then run clear ip ospf process.
Enter router-id 10.0.0.2 under router ospf 1; the new ID takes effect immediately.
Configure interface Loopback0 with the address 10.0.0.2 255.255.255.255.
Change R2's process to router ospf 2 so that it differs from R1's process.
explanation: Both routers use router ID 10.0.0.1, and OSPF neighbors must have unique router IDs, as the DUP_RTRID_NBR message shows. A new router-id command does not take effect until the OSPF process restarts, so it must be followed by clear ip ospf process (or a reload). A loopback address is ignored while a router-id command is configured, and process IDs are only locally significant.

Longest prefix match picks the OSPF /29, so the route in use has AD 110, the first number in [110/4]. The lower ADs of the static route (5) and EIGRP (90) do not matter, because they belong to shorter prefixes.

stem: A branch has two gateway routers. The team wants both routers to forward user traffic at the same time while every host keeps the same default gateway address, without splitting hosts into separate groups or DHCP scopes. Which first hop redundancy protocol meets this requirement?
choices: GLBP
HSRP version 2
VRRP
HSRP with preempt enabled on both routers
explanation: In GLBP the active virtual gateway (AVG) answers ARP requests for the single virtual IP with different virtual MAC addresses, each owned by an active virtual forwarder (AVF), so several routers forward at once. HSRP and VRRP have only one forwarding router per group; sharing load with them requires several groups and different gateway addresses for different hosts. Preempt only decides which router is active, not how many forward.

stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)
exhibit:
R1# show ip route 10.70.0.0
Routing entry for 10.70.0.0/16
  Known via "ospf 1", distance 110, metric 3, type intra area
  Last update from 10.0.13.3 on GigabitEthernet0/2, 00:15:41 ago
  Routing Descriptor Blocks:
  * 10.0.12.2, from 7.7.7.7, 00:15:41 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/1
      Route metric is 3, traffic share count is 1
    10.0.13.3, from 7.7.7.7, 00:15:41 ago, via GigabitEthernet0/2
      Route metric is 3, traffic share count is 1
choices: R1 has two equal-cost paths to 10.70.0.0/16.
The route's administrative distance is 110.
If GigabitEthernet0/1 goes down, R1 still has a route to 10.70.0.0/16 through 10.0.13.3.
The metric of 3 means that the network is three router hops away.
The route was learned from a different OSPF area.
Only 10.0.12.2 is used for forwarding, because the asterisk marks the single active path.
explanation: Two routing descriptor blocks with the same metric are equal-cost paths, and distance 110 is OSPF's AD. Losing one path leaves the other installed. The metric is the cumulative OSPF cost, not a hop count, and type intra area means the prefix is in R1's own area. The asterisk only marks which path the next process-switched packet would use; with CEF, traffic is shared across both paths.

stem: All four routers run OSPF with default settings. R1 shares traffic for 10.80.0.0/24 across both paths, even though one path crosses a 100 Mbps link. Which change makes R1 prefer the all-gigabit path through R2 while keeping OSPF cost based on bandwidth across the network?
exhibit:
R1 Gi0/1 (1 Gbps)    ---  Gi0/0 R2
R2 Gi0/1 (1 Gbps)    ---  Gi0/1 R4
R1 Gi0/2 (1 Gbps)    ---  Gi0/0 R3
R3 Fa0/1 (100 Mbps)  ---  Fa0/1 R4
R4 Gi0/0 (1 Gbps)    ---  LAN 10.80.0.0/24

R1# show ip route ospf | begin 10.80
O        10.80.0.0/24 [110/3] via 10.0.13.3, 00:07:02, GigabitEthernet0/2
                      [110/3] via 10.0.12.2, 00:07:02, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: Configure auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 under router ospf on all four routers.
Configure bandwidth 1000000 on the FastEthernet interfaces of R3 and R4.
Configure maximum-paths 1 under router ospf on R1.
Configure ip ospf cost 1 on R1's GigabitEthernet0/1.
explanation: With the default 100 Mbps reference bandwidth, both FastEthernet and Gigabit interfaces cost 1, so both paths total 3. A 1000 Mbps reference makes Gigabit cost 1 and FastEthernet cost 10, giving 3 through R2 and 12 through R3; it should be set the same on every router. Raising the FastEthernet bandwidth value makes that slow link look faster, maximum-paths 1 keeps one path but not necessarily the right one, and Gi0/1 already costs 1.

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.0.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
      172.16.0.0/16 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        172.16.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        172.16.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
S     192.168.99.0/24 is directly connected, Serial0/1/0
      192.168.100.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.100.0/30 is directly connected, Serial0/1/0
L        192.168.100.1/32 is directly connected, Serial0/1/0
choices: It is a static route configured with only an exit interface, so R1 sends matching packets straight out Serial0/1/0.
It is a subnet configured on Serial0/1/0, so R1 owns an address in 192.168.99.0/24.
It was learned dynamically from the router at the other end of Serial0/1/0.
It is a host route, because no next-hop address is listed.
explanation: The code S marks a static route, and is directly connected with no next hop means it was configured with an exit interface only, such as ip route 192.168.99.0 255.255.255.0 Serial0/1/0. A connected subnet would use the code C with a matching L entry, which this prefix does not have. Static routes are not learned from neighbors, and a host route would be a /32, not a /24.

stem: R4 learns its IPv6 default route from OSPFv3. Enter the global configuration command that creates a backup IPv6 default static route through the next hop 2001:DB8:F00D::1 with an administrative distance of 200.
explanation: The IPv6 default route is ::/0, and the distance goes after the next hop, so ipv6 route ::/0 2001:DB8:F00D::1 200 creates it. Because 200 is higher than OSPFv3's 110, the route floats and is installed only if the OSPFv3 default disappears. A global unicast next hop does not need an exit interface; only a link-local next hop does.

stem: R1 and R2 share VLAN 10 and can ping each other's GigabitEthernet0/1 addresses, yet both report themselves as the active HSRP router for 10.10.10.1. Which change resolves the problem?
exhibit:
R1# show standby GigabitEthernet0/1 | include Group|State|Virtual IP|Standby router
GigabitEthernet0/1 - Group 10 (version 2)
  State is Active
  Virtual IP address is 10.10.10.1
  Standby router is unknown

R2# show standby GigabitEthernet0/1 | include Group|State|Virtual IP|Standby router
GigabitEthernet0/1 - Group 10
  State is Active
  Virtual IP address is 10.10.10.1
  Standby router is unknown
choices: Configure standby version 2 on R2's GigabitEthernet0/1.
Configure standby 10 preempt on both routers.
Configure standby 10 priority 110 on R1.
Change R2's virtual IP to 10.10.10.254 so that the routers no longer conflict.
explanation: R1 runs HSRP version 2 and R2 runs the default version 1. Version 1 hellos go to 224.0.0.2 and version 2 hellos go to 224.0.0.102 in a different format, so neither router hears the other, and each becomes active with no standby. Priority and preempt matter only after the routers exchange hellos, and a different virtual IP would break the shared gateway instead of fixing it.

stem: R5 and R6 connect over a dedicated Ethernet link, and both routers have the configuration shown on their link interfaces. Which statement about this link is true?
exhibit:
R5# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip address 10.5.6.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
 ip ospf 1 area 0
end

R5# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
6.6.6.6           0   FULL/  -        00:00:35    10.5.6.2        GigabitEthernet0/0/1
choices: No DR or BDR is elected on the link, so the routers become fully adjacent without waiting for an election.
The hello and dead timers change to 30 and 120 seconds.
R6 can never become fully adjacent with R5, because its priority is 0.
Ethernet supports only the broadcast network type, so the routers still hold a DR/BDR election.
explanation: The point-to-point network type skips the DR/BDR election and its wait timer, which is why the neighbor shows FULL/- . Its timers stay at 10 and 40 seconds; 30 and 120 belong to NBMA network types. The Pri column shows 0 because priority has no meaning on a point-to-point link, not because the adjacency is blocked. IOS lets you set point-to-point on an Ethernet interface, and it is a common choice for two-router links.

stem: R1 can ping the server, but PC1 cannot. Which command fixes the problem?
choices: On R3: ip route 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/0
explanation: R1's own ping is sourced from its exit interface, 10.0.12.1, and R3 has a route back to 10.0.12.0/30, so it succeeds. R3 has no route to 192.168.1.0/24, so replies to PC1 are dropped; the static route via R2 (10.0.23.1) fixes the return path. The R2 option would add a second, equal static route pointing back toward R3 and break traffic. R1 already has a specific route, and pointing R3's route out its LAN interface sends the replies the wrong way.

stem: R9 runs OSPF and currently uses router ID 10.9.9.9, taken from Loopback0. An engineer adds interface Loopback1 with the address 192.168.99.9 and then enters router-id 9.9.9.9 under router ospf 1. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)
choices: R9 keeps using 10.9.9.9 until the OSPF process is reset or the router reloads.
After clear ip ospf process, R9 uses 9.9.9.9.
R9 immediately changes its router ID to 192.168.99.9, because Loopback1 now has the highest loopback address.
After a reload, R9 uses 192.168.99.9, because loopback addresses take precedence over the router-id command.
R9's neighbors must be configured with the new router ID before the adjacencies can come back up.
explanation: The router ID is chosen when the OSPF process starts, so neither the new loopback nor the router-id command changes it on a running process. Once the process restarts, through clear ip ospf process or a reload, the manually configured 9.9.9.9 wins, because the router-id command outranks any loopback address. Neighbors learn router IDs dynamically from hellos and need no changes.

stem: What does the second entry in the exhibit represent?
exhibit:
R6# show ip route | include 10.6.6
C        10.6.6.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
L        10.6.6.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/3
choices: The IPv4 address configured on R6's GigabitEthernet0/3 interface
A static host route to a device attached to GigabitEthernet0/3
An address that R6 learned through ARP on GigabitEthernet0/3
A route that R6 advertises to its OSPF neighbors in place of the /24 subnet
explanation: An L (local) entry is a /32 for an address configured on one of the router's own interfaces; the C entry is the subnet attached to that interface. A static host route would use the code S. ARP entries live in the ARP table, not the routing table, and routing protocols advertise the connected subnet, not the local /32.

stem: R1, R2 and R3 share VLAN 100. R1 is fully adjacent with R2, but neither R1 nor R2 lists R3 as a neighbor. Which command on R3's GigabitEthernet0/0 fixes the problem?
exhibit:
R1# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0 | include State|Timer|Neighbor Count
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
  Neighbor Count is 1, Adjacent neighbor count is 1

R3# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.100.0.3/24, Area 0, Attached via Interface Enable
  Process ID 1, Router ID 3.3.3.3, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DROTHER, Priority 0
  No designated router on this network
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 30, Wait 30, Retransmit 5
  (output omitted)
  Neighbor Count is 0, Adjacent neighbor count is 0
choices: ip ospf dead-interval 40
ip ospf priority 1
ip ospf hello-interval 10
ip ospf network point-to-point
explanation: R3's dead interval is 30 while R1 (and R2) use 40, and both the hello and dead intervals must match, so the hellos are rejected. Priority 0 only keeps R3 out of the DR/BDR roles; a priority-0 router still becomes FULL with the DR and BDR. The hello interval is already 10, and point-to-point is the wrong network type for a segment with three routers.

stem: Match each static route command to the type of route it creates.
pairs: IPv4 network route with the default static AD
explanation: A default route matches everything: 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 in IPv4 and ::/0 in IPv6. A host route matches one address: 255.255.255.255 (/32) in IPv4 or /128 in IPv6. A network route matches a subnet, and adding a distance higher than the primary route's AD (here 130) turns it into a floating static backup. Without a distance, a static route uses AD 1.

stem: R1's GigabitEthernet0/0, which connects to the ISP router at 203.0.113.1, goes down/down. R1 has no other default route. What happens to R2's default route?
exhibit:
R1 (Internet edge)
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0
 default-information originate

R2# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       * - candidate default (remaining codes omitted)

Gateway of last resort is 10.0.12.1 to network 0.0.0.0

O*E2  0.0.0.0/0 [110/1] via 10.0.12.1, 03:10:22, GigabitEthernet0/0
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 5 subnets, 3 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.12.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.11.0.0/24 [110/2] via 10.0.12.1, 03:10:22, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.22.0.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.22.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: R2 removes it, because R1 stops advertising a default route once R1's own default route leaves its routing table.
R2 keeps it, because default-information originate advertises a default route even when R1 has none.
R2 keeps it until R2 reloads, because OSPF external routes never age out on their own.
R2 keeps it but changes its metric to 16777215 to show that the path is unusable.
explanation: When Gi0/0 goes down, its connected subnet disappears, the static default's next hop can no longer be resolved, and the static route is removed. Without the always keyword, default-information originate advertises a default only while the ASBR has one in its own table, so R1 flushes its external LSA and R2 loses the O*E2 route and its gateway of last resort. Adding always would keep advertising the default even with no exit, which can black-hole traffic.

stem: Users on the 192.168.50.0/24 LAN cannot reach any Internet site. The default route works when the engineer pings 8.8.8.8 sourced from 198.51.100.2. Based on the exhibit, what is the cause?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | section interface|nat|access-list
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description LAN
 ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description ISP
 ip address 198.51.100.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat inside
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
access-list 1 permit 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255

R1# show ip nat translations
R1#
choices: ACL 1 uses the wrong wildcard mask for the LAN subnet.
The ip nat inside and ip nat outside commands are applied to the wrong interfaces.
The overload keyword can be used only with a NAT pool, not with an interface.
ACL 1 must be an extended ACL to match traffic for PAT.
explanation: Inside source NAT translates packets that arrive on an interface marked ip nat inside and leave an interface marked ip nat outside. Here the LAN interface is marked outside and the ISP interface inside, so LAN traffic never matches the rule and the translation table stays empty. The wildcard 0.0.0.255 correctly matches 192.168.50.0/24, overload with the interface keyword is the standard PAT form, and a standard ACL is the normal way to identify inside local addresses.

stem: Match each NAT command to the behavior it produces.
pairs: One inside host permanently mapped to one public address for all traffic
ip nat inside source static tcp 10.1.1.5 443 203.0.113.5 443
Only one TCP service on one inside host published on a public address
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB
Each inside host borrows its own public address from a pool until the entry times out
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB overload
Many inside hosts share the pool addresses, told apart by port numbers
ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/1 overload
Many inside hosts share the outside interface address, told apart by port numbers
explanation: The static keyword creates a permanent entry; adding a protocol and ports turns it into static PAT (port forwarding) for one service. A list plus pool without overload is dynamic NAT, which is one-to-one and limited by pool size. Adding overload makes it PAT, either with pool addresses or with the address of the named outside interface. Remember that only the overload keyword lets many inside hosts share one public address.

stem: Access switch SW5 is configured with an ntp server command that points to R2. After SW5 synchronizes, what stratum will show ntp status on SW5 report?
exhibit:
R2# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 4, reference is 10.10.10.1

R2# show ntp associations

  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~10.10.10.1      172.16.200.5     3     41     64   377  1.204  -0.311   0.880
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured
explanation: An NTP client is always one stratum higher (one hop further from the reference) than the server it syncs to. R2 syncs to 10.10.10.1 at stratum 3, so R2 is stratum 4, and SW5 syncing to R2 becomes stratum 5. A synchronized Cisco NTP client also answers other clients, so R2 needs no extra command to serve SW5.

stem: PC-7 receives its addressing from R1. The company DNS server is 10.50.1.53, and the security standard does not allow routers to run DNS services. Based on the exhibit, which change fixes name resolution for PC-7 and the rest of the VLAN?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | section dhcp
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.20.30.1 10.20.30.20
ip dhcp pool USERS
 network 10.20.30.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.20.30.1
 dns-server 10.20.30.1
 domain-name corp.example

C:\> ipconfig /all   (excerpt)
   IPv4 Address . . . : 10.20.30.57
   Subnet Mask  . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway  . : 10.20.30.1
   DHCP Server  . . . : 10.20.30.1
   DNS Servers  . . . : 10.20.30.1

C:\> ping 10.50.1.53
Reply from 10.50.1.53: bytes=32 time=2ms TTL=126

C:\> ping intranet.corp.example
Ping request could not find host intranet.corp.example.
choices: Change the default-router option in pool USERS to 10.50.1.53.
Enter ip domain-lookup on R1 so it can resolve names for the clients.
Replace dns-server 10.20.30.1 with dns-server 10.50.1.53 in pool USERS, then renew the client leases.
Remove 10.20.30.1 from the excluded-address range so the DHCP server can lease it.
explanation: DHCP hands clients the DNS server address, and this pool gives out the router's own address, which does not answer DNS queries. IP reachability to 10.50.1.53 works, so only the DNS option is wrong; pointing the option at the real server and renewing leases fixes every client. The default gateway must stay on the local subnet, ip domain-lookup only lets the router itself resolve names (and is on by default), and the excluded range protects the gateway address from being leased.

stem: A monitoring team is adding branch routers to its SNMP platform. Which two statements correctly describe SNMP operation? (Choose two.)
choices: The agent on the router sends Trap messages to the manager on UDP port 162.
The manager reads MIB variables from the agent with Get requests sent to UDP port 161.
SNMPv2c protects the community string by hashing it with MD5.
The manager acknowledges each Trap, so the agent retransmits any Trap that is lost.
The MIB is stored only on the NMS, and agents query it to learn what to report.
explanation: Managers poll agents with Get (and change values with Set) on UDP 161, and agents send unsolicited notifications to the manager on UDP 162. SNMPv1 and v2c send the community string in clear text; only SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption. Traps are not acknowledged; the Inform message, added in v2c, is the acknowledged notification. Each agent holds its own MIB variables, which the NMS reads.

stem: An engineer applies the configuration in the exhibit. Which two of these messages will R1 send to the syslog server? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1(config)# logging host 10.9.9.50
R1(config)# logging trap warnings
choices: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/2, changed state to down
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/2, changed state to down
%SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by netops on vty0 (10.9.9.14)
%SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list 101 denied tcp 10.9.9.77(51522) -> 10.1.1.1(23), 1 packet
%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on GigabitEthernet0/1 (1), with SW2 GigabitEthernet0/1 (99).
explanation: The number between the hyphens in a message is its severity. logging trap warnings sends level 4 (warnings) and everything more severe (levels 0 to 3). The LINK-3 (errors) and CDP-4 (warnings) messages qualify. LINEPROTO-5 and SYS-5 are notifications and SEC-6 is informational, so they are filtered out; the default trap level is informational (6), which would have included them.

stem: PCs in VLAN 20 show addresses in 169.254.0.0/16. The DHCP server at 10.99.0.10 has a scope for 10.2.20.0/24 with gateway 10.2.20.1 and is reachable from R1. Which change lets the VLAN 20 clients get addresses?
exhibit:
PC-A (VLAN 20) --- SW1 --- trunk --- R1 Gi0/0.20      R1 Gi0/1 --- DHCP server 10.99.0.10

R1# show running-config | section interface
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 10.2.20.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.99.0.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.99.0.10
choices: Move ip helper-address 10.99.0.10 from Gi0/1 to subinterface Gi0/0.20.
Add ip helper-address 10.2.20.1 under Gi0/1 so replies return to the VLAN.
Change the scope's default gateway on the server to 10.99.0.1.
Configure ip dhcp pool VLAN20 on R1 with network 10.99.0.0 255.255.255.0.
explanation: ip helper-address must be on the interface that receives the client broadcasts, which is the VLAN 20 subinterface. There R1 turns the DHCPDISCOVER into a unicast to the server and sets giaddr to 10.2.20.1, which tells the server which scope to use. On Gi0/1 the helper never sees the VLAN 20 broadcasts. The client gateway must stay 10.2.20.1, and a local pool for 10.99.0.0/24 would hand out the wrong subnet.

stem: A site buys a 200 Mbps CIR Metro Ethernet service delivered on a 1 Gbps port. The provider drops any traffic above the CIR. The site wants bursts above 200 Mbps to be delayed in its own router's buffers instead of being dropped by the provider. Which QoS tool should be applied outbound on the site router's WAN interface?
choices: Policing at 200 Mbps
Shaping at 200 Mbps
Marking all traffic with DSCP EF
Classification with NBAR and no other action
explanation: Shaping holds traffic that exceeds the configured rate in a queue and sends it later, which smooths the flow to the CIR and avoids the provider's policer. Policing at the same rate would drop or re-mark the excess on the site router, the very loss the site wants to avoid. Marking and classification only identify traffic; they do not control the rate. The usual design is shaping on the customer edge and policing on the provider edge.

stem: Engineers cannot open SSH sessions to R1. Based on the exhibit, which two global configuration commands should the engineer enter so that the SSH login with the netops account succeeds? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1# show running-config (excerpt)
hostname R1
no ip domain lookup
username netops privilege 15 secret 9 $9$Wv1...
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

R1# show ip ssh
SSH Disabled - version 1.99
% Please create RSA Keys to enable SSH (of at least 768 bits size) to enable SSH v2.

R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
% Please define a domain-name first.
choices: ip domain-name corp.example
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
ip domain lookup
enable secret Str0ngEnable!
explanation: IOS names the RSA key pair from the hostname and domain name, so it refuses to generate keys until a domain name exists; once the key exists, SSH is enabled. The vty lines already require SSH and local login, and the user is privilege 15. ip ssh version 2 only restricts the version (1.99 already accepts v2 clients), ip domain lookup is DNS resolution and is unrelated to key generation, and an enable secret is not needed for a privilege 15 user to log in.

stem: An engineer must copy a new IOS XE image from a file server to 40 routers. The security team requires that the server authenticate each transfer with a username and password and that the transfer use a reliable transport. Which protocol meets both requirements?
choices: TFTP, because it runs over TCP port 69 and the server checks a username and password
FTP, because it requires a login and runs over TCP
TFTP, because the router sends its hostname as the user name
SNMP, using Set requests to write the image to flash
explanation: FTP runs over TCP (port 21 for control, plus a separate data connection) and requires a username and password, which IOS can supply with ip ftp username and ip ftp password or in the URL. TFTP runs over UDP port 69 (not TCP) and has no user authentication at all, so it fails the login requirement; it does acknowledge each data block, but that is its own simple retransmission scheme, not a login. The hostname is not sent as a user name. SNMP is a management protocol, not an image transfer method.

stem: Interfaces on R1 already have ip nat inside and ip nat outside applied correctly. The internal web server 10.8.0.25 must be reachable from the Internet at 203.0.113.25 on every port, and the server must always appear as 203.0.113.25 when it opens outbound connections. Enter the global configuration command.
explanation: Static NAT, ip nat inside source static <inside local> <inside global>, creates a permanent two-way one-to-one mapping. Inbound connections to 203.0.113.25 reach the server, and its outbound traffic is always translated to that address. A static PAT entry (with tcp and port numbers) would publish only one service, and dynamic NAT or PAT entries exist only after the inside host starts a connection.

stem: About 300 users sit behind R1. Early in the morning a few users browse the Internet without trouble, but later most users cannot reach any external site. Based on the exhibit, which change fixes the problem?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ip nat|access-list
 ip nat inside
 ip nat outside
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.33 203.0.113.38 netmask 255.255.255.248
ip nat inside source list 10 pool PUBLIC
access-list 10 permit 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255

R1# show ip nat statistics (excerpt)
Total active translations: 6 (0 static, 6 dynamic; 0 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Hits: 48211  Misses: 913
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 10 pool PUBLIC refcount 6
 pool PUBLIC: netmask 255.255.255.248
        start 203.0.113.33 end 203.0.113.38
        type generic, total addresses 6, allocated 6 (100%), misses 913
choices: Change the pool netmask to 255.255.255.224 so more addresses are available.
Change the ACL 10 wildcard mask to 0.0.0.255.
Add the overload keyword to the ip nat inside source list 10 pool PUBLIC command.
Apply ip nat inside to GigabitEthernet0/1 as well.
explanation: Without overload this is dynamic NAT, which maps one inside host to one pool address, so only six users can be translated at a time; the 100% allocation and growing misses confirm the pool is exhausted. Adding overload enables PAT, letting thousands of sessions share the six addresses by port number. The netmask only has to cover the start and end addresses (it does), the ACL already matches 10.1.0.0/16, and marking the outside interface as inside would break translation.

stem: Branch router R2 is configured with ntp server 10.0.0.1, which is a loopback on HQ router R1. R1 has no other NTP commands than the one shown. Which statement is true after R2 synchronizes?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ntp
ntp server 192.0.2.123

R1# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 2, reference is 192.0.2.123
choices: R2 is stratum 3, and R1 answers R2's NTP requests without any additional command.
R2 is stratum 2, because a client copies the stratum of its server.
R1 must also be configured with ntp master before it will serve time to R2.
R1 must be configured with ntp peer 10.0.0.2 so that R2 can poll it.
explanation: A Cisco router configured with ntp server is a client of that server, and once synchronized it also acts as a server for other devices. R1 is stratum 2, so R2 becomes stratum 3, one higher than its source. ntp master is used only when a router should treat its own clock as authoritative (for example with no external source), and ntp peer creates symmetric peer mode, which is not needed for a client.

stem: An engineer mistypes a command on R1 and the console freezes for several seconds before printing the output in the exhibit. What explains this behavior?
exhibit:
R1# shwo ip route
Translating "shwo"...domain server (255.255.255.255)
% Unknown command or computer name, or unable to find computer address
choices: R1 is configured with no ip domain-lookup, so the parser waits for a lookup timer before it rejects the command.
R1 runs ip dns server and is forwarding the query to every host on the LAN.
DNS lookup is enabled by default and no name server is configured, so R1 treats the word as a host name and broadcasts a DNS query for it.
R1 is trying to download the command from a TFTP server because it is not in IOS.
explanation: IOS treats an unrecognized word at the EXEC prompt as a host name to Telnet to, and ip domain-lookup is enabled by default. With no ip name-server configured, the router sends the DNS query to the broadcast address and waits for it to time out. Entering no ip domain-lookup, or configuring a real name server, removes the delay. The Translating line proves that a lookup was attempted, so domain lookup is not disabled; ip dns server would make R1 answer queries rather than send them, and IOS does not fetch commands over TFTP.

stem: Match each SNMP version or security level to the protection it gives SNMP messages.
pairs: A shared community string sent in clear text
A user name only, with no message authentication and no encryption
Message authentication with a hash, but the payload is not encrypted
Message authentication plus encryption of the payload
distractors: Encryption of the payload without any authentication
explanation: SNMPv1 and v2c rely on community strings that cross the network unencrypted. SNMPv3 adds user-based security with three levels: noAuthNoPriv (user name match only), authNoPriv (HMAC authentication), and authPriv (authentication and encryption such as AES). There is no SNMPv3 level that encrypts without authenticating, so that option matches nothing.

stem: R1 already has logging host 10.9.9.50 configured. The operations team wants the server to receive severity 0 through 5 messages and nothing less severe. Enter the global configuration command (keyword or number form).
explanation: logging trap sets the most verbose severity sent to syslog servers, and the router sends that level plus all lower-numbered (more severe) levels. Level 5 is notifications, so logging trap notifications (or logging trap 5) sends levels 0 to 5. The default trap level is informational (6), which would also send level 6 messages.

stem: PC1 boots with no address. Put the events in the order they occur as PC1 obtains an address through R1.
exhibit:
PC1 (VLAN 30) --- SW1 --- R1 Gi0/0.30 10.3.30.1/24
                             R1 Gi0/1 10.99.0.1/24 --- DHCP server 10.99.0.10

interface GigabitEthernet0/0.30
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 10.3.30.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.99.0.10
items: PC1 broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER on VLAN 30.
R1 sets the giaddr field to 10.3.30.1 and forwards the Discover as a unicast to 10.99.0.10.
The server picks the 10.3.30.0/24 scope based on giaddr and sends a DHCPOFFER to 10.3.30.1.
R1 forwards the Offer onto VLAN 30 to PC1.
PC1 broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST for the offered address.
The server's DHCPACK is relayed by R1, and PC1 starts using the address.
explanation: The client always starts with a broadcast Discover, which a router would normally drop. The helper address makes R1 a relay agent: it unicasts the message to the server and records the receiving interface address in giaddr, which the server uses to choose the matching scope. Replies return to the relay, which forwards them onto the client VLAN. The Request and Ack follow the same relay path, completing Discover, Offer, Request, Ack.

stem: The policy in the exhibit is applied to a congested WAN link. Which statement describes how traffic is treated while GigabitEthernet0/1 is congested?
exhibit:
policy-map WAN-EDGE
 class VOICE
  priority percent 20
 class CRITICAL-DATA
  bandwidth percent 30
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 service-policy output WAN-EDGE
choices: VOICE packets are sent ahead of all other queues, and VOICE is held to 20 percent so it cannot starve the other classes.
CRITICAL-DATA can never use more than 30 percent of the link, even when the other classes are idle.
VOICE and CRITICAL-DATA are served in round robin with equal shares, because both have bandwidth reservations.
The policy marks VOICE packets with DSCP EF before they are queued.
explanation: The priority command creates a low latency queue (LLQ) that is always serviced first, and during congestion an implicit policer limits it to the configured 20 percent. The bandwidth command is CBWFQ: it guarantees CRITICAL-DATA at least 30 percent during congestion, and the class may use more when bandwidth is free. The priority queue is not part of the round robin, and the policy has no set command, so it does not mark anything; it relies on earlier classification and marking.

stem: A security review shows the output in the exhibit and requires that R1 accept only SSH version 2. Enter the global configuration command.
exhibit:
R1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 1.99
Authentication methods:publickey,keyboard-interactive,password
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3
explanation: Version 1.99 means the router accepts both SSHv1 and SSHv2 clients. ip ssh version 2 restricts it to SSHv2, which needs an RSA key of at least 768 bits (2048 is the common choice). The vty lines should also use transport input ssh so Telnet is refused.

stem: An engineer is choosing between TFTP and FTP to back up router configurations. Which two statements correctly describe TFTP compared with FTP? (Choose two.)
choices: TFTP uses UDP port 69.
TFTP has no user authentication.
TFTP uses separate TCP control and data connections.
TFTP lets the client list and browse the server's directories.
TFTP encrypts the file contents, while FTP sends them in clear text.
